Fit Guide

GET THE FIT RIGHT THE FIRST TIME.

Dog gear fit is about body measurements, not breed names. A "medium" varies by brand — measure your dog first.

Fit matters in dog gear more than most people expect. A pack that sits too far forward shifts all the weight onto the shoulders instead of the ribcage, where dogs are actually built to carry it. After 3 miles, you'll know — the dog will start shouldering it differently, and the straps will have worked their way out of adjustment. A harness that's too loose doesn't stay on during a steep descent and won't hold if a dog goes into the water unexpectedly.

All measurements should be taken while your dog is standing on a level surface with weight on all four legs. Use a flexible tape measure. Girth is the most important single measurement — it's the circumference of the ribcage at its widest point, just behind the front legs. Neck is measured at the base, where a collar sits. Back length runs from the base of the neck collar to the base of the tail. Weight is useful as a secondary check but should not be the primary sizing method, since two dogs of the same weight can have very different proportions.

When you're between sizes, go up. A slightly larger vest can be adjusted at the straps. A slightly larger boot can be secured with the fastening system. A too-small pack cannot be adjusted into fit — it will sit wrong regardless, cut into the shoulders, and restrict breathing on uphills. Double-coated breeds (Husky, Samoyed, Bernese, Golden) should add 1 inch to their girth measurement before selecting a size. Puppies under 12 months should wait for a stable adult size before fitting for a trail pack.

Measure girth at the widest part of the ribcage, just behind the front legs, while your dog is standing. This is the most important measurement for packs, vests, and harnesses — everything else is secondary to getting this right.

For boots, measure paw width with the dog standing on a piece of paper — trace around the outside of the paw at its widest point with weight fully on it. Measure all four paws; sizes often differ slightly. Use the widest measurement to select boot size.

When between sizes, always go up. A slightly larger harness can be tightened via the adjustment straps. A too-small pack compresses the chest and shifts weight forward after 2 miles — there is no way to adjust past a fundamental size mismatch.

HOW TO MEASURE YOUR DOG

Take measurements while your dog is standing on a flat surface. Use a flexible fabric tape measure.

Step 1

Girth

Wrap the tape around the widest part of the ribcage, just behind the front legs. Take the measurement while your dog is standing with weight on all four legs. Add 1 inch if your dog has a thick double coat. This measurement determines harness size, vest size, and pack size.

Step 2

Neck

Measure at the base of the neck where a collar naturally sits. This determines harness neck fit and coat neckline sizing. The measurement should allow two fingers of clearance — if the tape feels snug, add half an inch.

Step 3

Back Length

Measure from the base of the neck (where the collar sits) to the base of the tail. Do not include the tail itself. This measurement determines coat length and pack back length. Take the measurement along the top of the spine, not diagonally across the body.

Boot Sizing Only

Paw Width

Place a piece of paper under your dog's paw while they stand normally with full weight on it. Trace a line along the widest point of the paw — usually across the widest toe spread. Measure the distance across. Repeat on all four paws and use the widest measurement to select boot size. Paw sizes vary more than most people expect across the four legs.
